notes: The baseline has implemented capture and input interfaces, X11/Xfce backends, a browser H.264 viewer, bounded transport flow, a typed Node SDK and CLI. It is a local experimental framework, not feature parity with the comparison products.

The runnable baseline starts plain XFCE without the benchmark application. The comparison image bundled the fixture; both images contain an identical native executable and installed package database. Existing benchmark callers explicitly inject the same fixture, and that startup branch is verified separately. Real-application comparisons include the same inactive benchmark application in the background for all engines; do not treat them as measurements of a clean default desktop.

Real Thunar scroll medians (native / Selkies / KasmVNC): CPU 13.4% / 48.5% / 12.1%, RAM 166.0 MiB / 238.4 MiB / 179.8 MiB, container transmit 1.02 Mbps / 1.35 Mbps / 0.96 Mbps. Native has lower RAM in this workload; CPU, bandwidth and settled quality must be compared separately. Scroll pixel-change frequency is an activity diagnostic, not a smoothness ranking.

Real Freedoom turn/fire medians (native / Selkies / KasmVNC): CPU 100.9% / 72.8% / 103.7%, RAM 200.0 MiB / 267.1 MiB / 204.6 MiB, container transmit 38.55 Mbps / 5.85 Mbps / 83.02 Mbps. Selkies uses less CPU and bandwidth than native here; native transmits substantially less than KasmVNC. Motion fidelity is unmeasured in this application, so these are operating points rather than equal-quality efficiency rankings.

The limited-bandwidth synthetic video case remains a weakness: native median frozen PSNR 14.22 dB versus Selkies 34.62 dB, sparse matched-motion median PSNR 18.64 versus 21.58 dB, and input p95 210.1 versus 109.7 ms. Native has three sessions; Selkies has one. Only 11–12 native motion pairs and 24 Selkies pairs matched, so inspect coverage counters and raw evidence. These are not quality-matched comparisons; preserving delivered update rate has not solved fidelity or tail latency.

Real Thunar and Freedoom sessions are reported separately from custom synthetic diagnostics. Each real-application engine has three fresh sessions. The Thunar data are identical real files with checked hashes; actual X11 content and decoded correspondence validate navigation and scrolling. Game checks independently observe held/released native keys and live pixels; they do not establish equal gaming fidelity or input latency.

Three general-engine variants were measured. Variant 1 introduced bounded pipelining and adaptive VBV; variant 2 repaired cap-relative recovery; variant 3 corrected two congestion masks caused by queue-inflated RTT and an excessive queued-byte guard. The final core is frozen at 143d4ee. No workload names appear in engine policy. Additional time after the original two-hour optimization window is validation requested by the user, not unbounded variant tuning.

The final original-fixture median is 50.36 visible updates/s against 50.78 producer updates/s; input p95 43.4 ms, CPU 40.2% of one core, RAM 146.4 MiB, container TX 1.27 Mbps. Quiescent idle CPU is 3.26%. The 60 FPS configuration is not proof of sustained 60 FPS.

The broader synthetic fixture targets 30 Hz and usually produces 27–29 updates/s. Its idle case includes marker damage and is not quiescent idle. Local references have n=1; the final candidate has n=3. The earlier original three-engine sessions are historical and not pooled with broad or real-application workloads.

Lower resource usage must be read with fidelity and latency. No universal winner, equal-quality result, held-out workload claim, WAN claim or Rust-versus-C++ performance claim follows from these measurements.
limitations: Transmit Mbps is container eth0 TX upstream of the relay, not browser-delivered goodput. Relay queues and socket buffers can skew finite windows. Controlled delay adds 25 ms each direction; limited profile also caps downstream at 8 Mbps and upstream at 2 Mbps.

The final native and refreshed network references use the same runner and current relay. Older network runs and invalid earlier window cases are retained in qualification/results but are not selected as final comparisons. Kasm local reference has the corrected visible-window fixture and an older runner lacking native telemetry; it remains n=1 diagnostic context.
Congestion backoff uses a 200 ms absolute age budget. Paths with high propagation delay can trigger conservative backoff; broader WAN policy remains work.

All selected raw JSON is exported below. Full image-pair sets and original logs remain in qualification/results and bench/results; representative captures are exported beside raw JSON. Missing image files in the compact export are not missing from the local measurement directories.

Game motion quality, real-application input latency, natural video, browser/editor workloads, prolonged soak, audio, clipboard, IME, resize, hardware encoding, Wayland and GNOME remain outside the verified baseline.

readerGuide.title: 1. The answer in plain English
paragraphs: We built a small engine that sends a Linux desktop to a web browser and sends keyboard and mouse input back. It works in the tested X11/XFCE environment. It is not yet proven rock solid, ready for public deployment, or a replacement for every feature in Selkies or KasmVNC.

The clearest positive result is low container memory use in real file-manager work. The clearest weakness is synthetic moving video on a restricted connection: image quality degrades and the slowest measured interactions take longer. The game test shows a different tradeoff: Selkies uses less CPU and bandwidth than our engine in that workload.

Read sections 1–4 for the main result. Sections 5–8 explain the measurements, test coverage, and reliability limits. The expandable tables retain every measured value, including ranges, missing metrics, and excluded observations. This revision explains existing evidence; it does not contain a new performance run.

readerGuide.title: 2. What happens when you use the desktop
paragraphs: The application and the streaming engine do different jobs. Chrome, Ghostty, Thunar, or a game runs inside Linux and draws into its desktop. The engine captures that desktop and transports the picture. The browser you use to view it decodes the picture. An application can exit while the desktop and stream keep running.

Picture path: application → X11 desktop → pixel capture → H.264 compression → WebSocket connection → browser video decoder → visible canvas. Input travels in the opposite direction: browser keyboard or pointer event → server → X11 input backend → application.

The current display is Xvfb, an X11 display kept in memory, with the XFCE desktop running on it. This allows a graphical session without a physical monitor. It does not prove behavior on a hardware display or on Wayland.

rows: Application
Produces the content you want to use.
Runs separately from the streaming engine; its own startup and resource needs still matter.
Capture
Reads the desktop pixels and detects changes.
CPU capture from X11 at a fixed 1280 × 720 resolution.
Encoder
Compresses many pixels into a smaller video stream.
Persistent libx264 through libavcodec; compression trades bandwidth against image detail.
Flow control
Stops old frames piling up when the receiver is slow.
Up to 8 outstanding frames and 8 MiB of logical encoded payload; these are not total-memory limits.
Transport and viewer
Moves the compressed picture and draws it locally.
WebSocket transport and browser H.264 VideoDecoder. Decode and drawing cost client resources too.
Input and cursor
Makes clicks, typing, and pointer shapes correspond to the remote desktop.
X11 input; the later cursor update sends images and hotspots separately from video. Cursor position follows the local pointer.
SDK and CLI
Lets a program request input or a screenshot.
Typed Node client and command-line tool. One browser or one agent owns input at a time; an ACK is submission, not proof an app completed the action.

readerGuide.title: 3. The results that matter most
paragraphs: These figures are medians across selected sessions. They describe the settings and workloads actually tested. They do not compare the engines at identical picture quality, so a lower resource number alone is not an efficiency win.

Thunar is a real file manager. Freedoom is a real game. Both have three fresh sessions per engine. The constrained-video diagnostic has three native sessions but only one Selkies session, which gives much less confidence about the reference engine’s run-to-run variation.

readerGuide.title: 4. What improved, and what still hurts
paragraphs: The first general variant allowed several frames to be in flight instead of waiting after each one, and adapted the encoder’s bitrate ceiling. The second repaired recovery relative to that ceiling. The third repaired two cases where queueing could hide congestion. The final core was then frozen for validation; it does not choose a policy by workload name.

In the synthetic scrolling test with added delay, the native final candidate delivered about 28.54 visible updates/s versus 14.58 for the earlier native reference. Their producers generated about 28.61 and 26.82 updates/s, respectively. This is a useful improvement under that test, with three candidate sessions and one reference session; it is not evidence for arbitrary internet paths.

For local synthetic video, transmit fell from about 45.45 to 18.60 Mbps and CPU from 70.51% to 60.46%, while frozen PSNR fell from 34.03 to 31.77 dB and sparse-motion PSNR from 33.56 to 30.42 dB. That is a bandwidth/quality tradeoff, not a free performance gain.

On the restricted video test, maintaining delivered updates did not preserve picture quality or input tail latency. The current policy has no enforced visual-quality floor or quiet-period refinement. Fixing this measured weakness should precede any claim of quality-matched superiority.

readerGuide.title: 5. How to read the numbers
paragraphs: A cell such as 43.200 [43.000–44.100], n=3 means: the middle result across three independent sessions was 43.2; the smallest was 43.0 and the largest was 44.1. The range is not a confidence interval. Different metrics can have different n because missing values are not replaced with zero.

A measurement of 0 is different from ‘unmeasured.’ A failed observation is different from a slow but valid one. Failed observations stay visible in the exclusion table and raw files. No selected KasmVNC result for a profile should be read as a score of zero.

rows: CPU (% of one core)
100% means roughly one fully occupied CPU core; values above 100% are possible.
Lower is better only for comparable delivered work and quality. This includes the desktop and app inside the container.
RAM (MiB)
The container memory measure used by the runner.
Does not include the viewing browser or the whole Docker VM. It is not the total cost of using the desktop.
Container transmit (Mbps)
Data sent from the container before the relay.
Not necessarily bytes delivered to the browser during the same interval; queues can distort short windows.
Producer versus visible updates/s
How often the test content changes versus how many distinct marked updates the viewer observes.
A 30 Hz producer cannot demonstrate sustained 60 FPS. These are not physical monitor presentation measurements.
Observed visual changes/s
How often sampled pixels change in a real application.
Useful to confirm activity; not decoded FPS or a smoothness score.
Input median and p95 (ms)
Typical measured response and the threshold containing about 95% of that session’s trials.
Lower is better. p95 is not a maximum or a guarantee about future clicks; the synthetic cases use 20 trials per workload.
PSNR (dB)
A pixel comparison; higher generally means closer to the reference.
Compare the same content and method. A difference in dB is not a percentage improvement and does not fully describe perceived quality.
MAE
Mean absolute pixel error; lower means closer to the reference.
Read with PSNR and the images. Whole-frame averages can hide small text or edge defects.
Frozen versus motion quality
Frozen compares a settled picture; motion compares sampled frames matched to the same source update.
They answer different questions. Neither sparse motion samples nor a sharp frozen screenshot prove full-rate motion quality.
Motion coverage
How many source and decoded samples could actually be paired.
Small matched sets limit conclusions, even if many frames were collected. Inspect pair counts and coverage together.

readerGuide.title: 6. What the experiment actually covered
paragraphs: The report selects 49 raw runs and records 3 excluded run/workload observations. The raw run identity, runner hash, fixture hash, and image are retained below. Selection is explicit; the exporter does not search for a best-looking run.

The comparison environment uses CPU capture at 1280 × 720, two allocated CPUs, a 1536 MiB container limit, 512 MiB shared memory, and Chrome 156 as viewer. These are benchmark conditions, not a promise that every application fits that resource budget.

The broader synthetic tests usually produced 27–29 updates/s against a 30 Hz target. Their ‘idle’ case still changed a marker and consumed work; the separate original quiescent-idle measurement was 3.26% CPU. Those two idle results must not be compared as if they were the same task.

The comparison images contain the same inactive benchmark application during real-app runs. The clean baseline starts plain XFCE; artifact-equivalence checks relate its native executable and package database to the measured image. The app comparisons are not measurements of a completely clean default desktop.

Resource sampling, settled-image comparison, sparse-motion comparison, and input checks are separate passes. Short controlled samples make differences inspectable, but they do not establish days of stability, natural-video quality, or performance in every browser.

readerGuide.title: 7. Is the engine reliable enough?
paragraphs: There is useful functional evidence, but production reliability is not established. Short passing tests show that the exercised paths worked under their conditions. They do not prove the absence of crashes, leaks, races, or application compatibility issues over long sessions.

The later cursor change passed 13 cursor, 12 video/input, and 5 framework checks in each of release and sanitizer builds: 60 checks total. Graceful shutdown exited zero, with no reported sanitizer diagnostics. System libraries were not instrumented. These are later correctness checks, not a rerun of the performance tables.

The engine bounds logical encoded data and has timeout and held-input cleanup behavior. Its frame-age thresholds are admission and recovery mechanisms, not hard guarantees on what the user sees: already queued or in-transit work may be older. Total memory also includes codecs, transport, applications, and the browser.

The current service has no authentication or TLS. Its documented deployment binds to host loopback for isolated local use. Anyone who can reach the service can observe and control the desktop; an Origin check is not a login or authorization system.

readerGuide.title: 8. What today’s installation issues do and do not tell us
paragraphs: Update dated October 27, 2026: the current interactive desktop is no longer the untouched benchmark snapshot. It has a later cursor build, Chrome and Ghostty installed, and a Chromium-compatible container seccomp profile. The benchmark numbers above were not rerun for this modified desktop.

The long installation was caused by building Ghostty from source, compiler memory kills, build retries, and saving/reconfiguring the container for Chrome’s sandbox. Chrome’s package installation itself was only part of that work. This was installation work sharing the machine’s resources, not a measurement of streaming latency or engine efficiency.

Ghostty was subsequently reported to exit unexpectedly. An isolated launch on a separate display reproduced an early process exit while the streaming process remained running. The current container’s memory counters showed no out-of-memory kills at the diagnostic check. The application-level cause remains unresolved; investigation was stopped at the user’s request. The earlier brief launch check does not establish application stability.

An app closing, the whole desktop session ending, and the viewer freezing are distinct failures. Diagnosis must check application exit status, container health, native-server state, and browser decode/draw progress. Continued streaming does not certify the application; an application exit alone does not establish an engine fault. No engine fix or new reliability certification is claimed by this report revision.

readerGuide.title: 9. What evidence would change the conclusion
paragraphs: The next work should turn specific unknowns into measured results. This is a proposed qualification sequence, not work already completed. Set acceptance criteria before each run, preserve failures, and compare the same source and environment.

First reproduce and resolve application exits such as Ghostty’s, separating app, graphics, container, and transport causes. Then address the measured constrained-video quality and input-tail weakness. Only after those checks pass should the report’s reliability language become stronger.

rows: Long-running sessions
Hours of application use, process health, memory growth, frame progress, and controlled shutdown.
Stability for the stated duration and workload, not an unlimited uptime guarantee.

Whether failure stays contained, recovers predictably, and releases held inputs.

Whether a resource advantage survives at comparable delivered quality.
Real network conditions
Loss, jitter, different propagation delays, bandwidth changes, and measured recovery times.
Behavior beyond the current controlled relay profiles.
Broader applications and clients
Browser, editor, terminal, natural video, more resolutions and intended architectures.
